paragraphs.text: Tim and his mom walked up to Aunt Rosa's house.
"I know this isn't ideal," Mom said, "but Aunt Rosa and I have to work Saturday shifts now. I don't want to leave you home alone."
"But why do I have to stay here with Andre?" Tim asked. "He's so much older than me, and we barely even talk when we see each other. All he does is stay in his room."
"You and your cousin might have more in common than you think," Mom said.
"I doubt it," Tim mumbled.
Inside the house Andre was nowhere to be seen. Tim plopped down on the sofa and turned on the TV. "Boring as usual," Tim thought.
"Yo," a voice said suddenly. "You play the piano, don't you?"
It was Andre. Tim looked at him, confused. "Yeah," Tim said. "Why?"
"Follow me."
Andre led Tim toward his room. Tim realized that he had never seen the inside of Andre's room before. Several Keep Out! stickers were crookedly plastered on the door.
"Welcome to my music studio," Andre said as they entered.

Tim blinked. It looked like a normal bedroom, not the studios he'd seen in music videos and on TV. The only musical things he saw were a piano keyboard and a mic connected to Andre's computer via USB cables.

"It probably doesn't look like much," Andre said, noticing Tim's reaction. "Many amateur musicians like me set up small home studios. Recording equipment and software aren't as expensive as most people would think."
"So you record yourself playing the piano and singing on your computer?" Tim asked.
"Sometimes," Andre said, "but I can do more than that. With my music program and this keyboard, I can pretty much play any sound I want—real instruments, electronic sounds, and even dog barks!"

Tim laughed. "Here, let me show you a song I've been working on." Andre opened a file on his music program. "First I came up with this melody. I played it on the keyboard and chose the sound I wanted to use."
Tim listened to Andre's electronic melody. "Is that the whole song?"

"No, that's just one track," Andre said. He pointed to some jagged lines on the computer screen. "Each instrument I use is on a separate track. After I made the first track, I added drums and bass." He played the individual tracks for Tim. "I can mix the tracks together to make the song." He pressed Play, and Tim heard all three tracks playing simultaneously.
Tim was surprised by how passionate Andre was about his music. He'd never seen this side of his cousin before. "That's so cool!" he exclaimed.

"Thanks," Andre said with a sigh. "But I'm not finished yet. That was just the verse portion of the song. I can't think of a catchy melody for the chorus—the part that repeats between verses. That's the part listeners will remember most. Do you think you can come up with something?"

"Me?" Tim asked nervously. He'd been playing the piano for seven years, but he'd never composed his own melodies before. "I guess I can try." He took a seat at the keyboard and listened to Andre's melody a few more times. He tried to imagine some possible melodies in his head. Then he put his fingers on the keys and started to play. "How about something like this?"

"Perfect!" Andre looked impressed. He played the chorus with Tim's melody mixed with the rest of the instruments. "Now I just need to arrange the parts into an introduction, verses, chorus, and an ending—sort of like the structure of an essay. I think I'll start it like this."
"What will you do when you're finished composing the song?" Tim asked.

"I'm going to rap over it and make a demo song. Then I'll upload it to the internet and send the link to major record labels. Maybe they'll give me advice. Or who knows, if I'm lucky, maybe one of them will offer me a contract."
"You know," Tim said, "I can sing too. What if you rap the verses and I sing the chorus?"
Andre's face lit up. "Great idea! Start writing your own lyrics for the chorus. I'll finish the song arrangement and write my lyrics too. Then we can record our vocals."
Tim grabbed a pencil and some paper. "I guess spending Saturdays with Andre will be pretty fun after all," he thought.
" Aloha !" Kaycee's grandparents called to Kaycee and Mom at the airport.
Grandma rushed over and draped purple orchid-blossom necklaces over their shoulders.
"The flowers mean 'welcome,'" Grandpa explained as he leaned closer to whisper. "It's rude to take the lei off until later."

As they walked to the car, Kaycee took in the palm trees and black lava rock walls. She sure wasn't in Texas anymore! Kaycee's relatives often visited the mainland, but this was Kaycee's first visit to Mom's home state of Hawaii.
"Wow," she thought. "I feel like I'm in a foreign country!"
At dinner everyone was talking a lot—and fast, sprinkling Hawaiian words into the conversation. Kaycee knew some words from Mom, but not all of them, which her cousin Bruce teased her for.
"We're having a family reunion luau tomorrow," Grandpa announced.
"A luau! I love parties!" Kaycee said.
"A luau has food, music, and dancing, but it's not just a party. It's a celebration of ohana ," Mom said.
"That means 'family,'" Bruce added.
"I actually know that one!" Kaycee shot back.
" Aloha —good morning!" Bruce greeted Kaycee after breakfast. "Let's go dig taro to make poi for tonight."

Kaycee didn't know what poi was, but she didn't want to ask Bruce. So she stayed quiet as she followed her cousin past a field of yams to a swampy area. They dug up taro roots, then stopped on the way back to help Uncle with the underground oven. A bed of banana stalks rested on red-hot rocks in the shallow pit. Kaycee watched as Bruce and Uncle lowered a whole pig into the pit. Then she helped them cover it with wet banana leaves.
"The pork will be ready by dinner," Uncle said.
In the house Grandma snacked on sugarcane as she finished steaming the freshly picked taro.
"We don't grow much sugarcane on the islands anymore," Grandma said. "But my family, like many of the first Asian immigrants to Hawaii, came to work on sugarcane plantations in the 1800s."
Kaycee pulled the tough skin off a steamed taro as they started to prepare the poi. "What's poi anyway?"
"It's mashed taro mixed with water," Grandma explained. "It's a staple food here on the islands."
Kaycee pounded the roots with a stone pestle as Grandma added water. Kaycee looked doubtfully at the smooth, purplish gray paste.
"It's good!" Mom promised. She dipped two fingers in and tasted it.
Kaycee tasted it just like Mom had. "Wow, it is delicious!"
That evening carloads of guests arrived, and people swarmed to welcome Kaycee and her mother. Ohana was not just relatives, Kaycee realized. It extended to friends.

Every guest had brought a special dish. Kaycee saw macaroni salad, Chinese steamed buns, and lots of fresh seafood. There was even Spam musubi—a rice and Spam snack that Mom often made. Uncle's steaming pork sat in the middle of the table, smelling delicious.

The sound of drums filled the night and guests hula danced. Auntie danced nearby as Grandfather plucked the strings of his ukulele. "Portuguese immigrants, like my family, brought the instrument to Hawaii in 1879," he explained. "The Hawaiians named it ukulele, which means 'jumping flea,' because of the way the musician's fingers jumped across the strings."
"Traditional hula only used drums," Auntie said. "Other instruments, like the ukulele, were added later. Originally, the dances told stories about the ancient gods."
Kaycee joined Auntie, swaying her hips and following the motions of Auntie's arms and hands. "Hey," she said suddenly. "This is like a Texas line dance! Just add a stomp, stomp, turn."
Everyone followed her example.
"You invented the first Texan hula line dance!" Bruce said.
Kaycee grinned. "I guess the islands are a part of me, and now I'm a part of the islands!"
"It's a perfect day to walk across the Brooklyn Bridge," Paul said.

He looked up at the enormous bridge that connected two very busy parts of New York City—Brooklyn and Manhattan. The bridge was pretty old now. But with its tall stone towers and strong-looking cables, it was still an amazing sight above the East River.
"Dad, who built this bridge?" Paul asked.

"A man named John Roebling," his father answered. "Now Brooklyn and Manhattan are part of the same city—New York. But they used to be two different cities. In the 1800s boats would bring people back and forth across the East River to work, shop, or visit friends. The river was sometimes rough, and the boats were often late. One day John was on one of those boats with his son, and he got the idea to build a suspension bridge across the river. Many people said it couldn't be done.

"But one winter the East River froze, and the boats couldn't get through. People from Brooklyn couldn't get to work in Manhattan. Finally it was decided that a bridge should be built, connecting the two places."
"Was John Roebling an engineer like you?" asked Paul.

"Yes, he was. His son, Washington, was an engineer too. In 1869 they started to work on the bridge together. But sadly, a freak accident happened. While John Roebling was on the Brooklyn side of the river, his foot got caught in the dock. An incoming boat crashed into the dock, injuring him badly. He died a month later. So Washington took over."
"Washington must have been sad when his father died," murmured Paul.

"Yes, he and his father were very close. But Washington was ready for the job. He started working right away, digging deep under the river mud to create supports for the two bridge towers. This almost cost him his life."
Paul gasped. "You mean, Washington almost died too?"

"Yes, he designed something called a caisson to use for the underwater project. These caissons, which prevented the water from flooding the work area, were filled with compressed air. And at the time, people didn't realize that working in compressed air can cause caisson disease, or decompression sickness. That's a dangerous condition that results from gas bubbles forming inside the body.

"Caisson disease affected Washington's nervous system, paralyzing him for a time and causing him great pain. Some members of his work crew even died from the illness! Washington never returned to the bridge, but he continued to manage the project. Imagine this—he used a telescope to watch the progress of the bridge construction from his home in Brooklyn!"
"Wow. It sounds like he was pretty sick—how could he manage everything from home?" Paul asked.

"Good question," his father said. "Washington's wife, Emily, helped him. She wrote his letters and helped with planning the work. She served as his eyes and ears, and delivered all his orders to the workers. She even studied complicated mathematics to learn more about building! Soon she earned the respect of everyone involved in the project. If it weren't for her, the Brooklyn Bridge probably wouldn't have been finished."
Paul's father pointed to the bridge towers. "When those towers were finished, they were 25 stories high, taller than any of the other buildings around them. Can you imagine that?"
Paul looked at the city skyline. All the huge skyscrapers made the bridge towers look small now. He tried to imagine how different the city must have looked back then.

"See those four main cables that run along the top from one tower to the other?" his father went on. "Can you spot all the wires hanging down from them? John Roebling invented their material, which is called wire rope. The wire rope is made of steel, so it is strong and can easily be bent into any shape. The Brooklyn Bridge was the first bridge where it was used.
"But those slanted supports were Washington's idea. He added them to make sure the bridge was safe."
"How long did it take to build the bridge?" asked Paul.
"Fourteen years," answered his father. "It was an amazing undertaking. When it was finished, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world.

"At the opening day ceremony in 1883, Emily Roebling was given the honor of being the first person to cross the bridge. She rode in a horse and carriage from the Brooklyn side to the Manhattan side. The workers all cheered as she went by."
"Her husband must have been proud," said Paul.

"Yes, it was his idea. Crowds lined the streets of Manhattan and Brooklyn, and hundreds of ships were packed into the East River. On the Manhattan side, the president of the United States waited with the governor and the mayor of New York City. Then they met Emily and they all walked across the bridge together. After the ceremony they went to the Roebling house to honor Washington and his father. There was a grand show of fireworks that night. It was the greatest celebration ever held in America up until that time."
"That sounds pretty cool," said Paul.
His father agreed with a nod.
"I'd like to help build a bridge like that one day," said Paul.

His father beamed. "The Brooklyn Bridge inspired the building of many other bridges, allowing people to travel easily to many new places. It was seen as the greatest engineering achievement of the nineteenth century."
"My teacher said the Brooklyn Bridge is a true American landmark." Paul grabbed his father's arm. "Come on, Dad! Let's see how fast we can get to the other side!"

Vatican City, or the Vatican, as it is commonly known, lies within the city of Rome. Despite its name, Vatican City is actually a country! This country is home to the leadership of the Catholic Church and has a rich history.

St. Peter's Basilica is its most famous site. The church was named for St. Peter, who was Jesus' favorite and most faithful follower. St. Peter was an early Christian leader in Rome. At that time, the Romans persecuted Christians. In the year 64, he was executed by Roman officials. He was buried in a graveyard on a hill called the Vatican.
As the number of Christians grew, a large church was built on the site where St. Peter was buried. Soon St. Peter's Basilica became the main church of the pope, the leader of the Catholic Church.

By 1506 St. Peter's Basilica was falling apart. It was also too small for all the church officials who worked there. So Pope Julius II demolished it and built a huge new church with a 42-meter-tall dome.

This new church was not fully completed until 1626. The new St. Peter's Basilica became the largest church in the world at the time. And because of its connection to St. Peter, it also became one of Christianity's most important churches. The church is still in use today.

Another famous religious building in the Vatican is the Sistine Chapel. The chapel was built between 1477 and 1481. The rectangular building looks plain and simple on the outside, but there is a treasure of Renaissance art inside.

Pope Julius II needed an artist to decorate the chapel's ceiling—all eight hundred square meters of it. He hired Michelangelo for the job, which was a surprising choice. Michelangelo was known for his sculpture, not his painting. For four years Michelangelo painted the ceiling with his head tilted up and his hands extended above his body. His labor was an amazing feat. The result was an even more amazing work of art.

The ceiling's nine main sections illustrate scenes from the Bible. Paintings of people and angels from the Bible decorate the borders. Thousands of tourists visit the Sistine Chapel each day to see Michelangelo's magnificent art.

Like St. Peter's Basilica, the Sistine Chapel is still used today. In fact, the chapel is used for one of the Catholic Church's most important ceremonies—the election of a new pope. When a pope dies or resigns, church officials called cardinals come to the Vatican to choose their new leader. The cardinals stay locked inside the Vatican. They have no contact with the outside world until they elect a new pope.

Every day during this time, the cardinals go into the Sistine Chapel. They pray about which cardinal should be the next pope. Then elections are held each day until a new pope is chosen. The cardinals vote by writing a name on a piece of paper. The votes are counted, and then all the ballots are burned in the chapel's furnace.

Outside the chapel, crowds gather, eagerly watching for signs of smoke from the chapel's chimney. Black smoke tells the crowd that the cardinals have not yet chosen a new pope. White smoke and the ringing of bells mean that a new pope has been elected. How is the black or white smoke made? In the past, wet straw was added to the fire to turn the smoke black. But sometimes the smoke looked gray instead of black or white. So nowadays chemicals are used to produce the black or white smoke.

After the election the new pope changes from his red cardinal's clothing into the white robes of the pope. Then he comes out and greets the people. He is now the leader of the Catholic Church—and a country, Vatican City.

Vatican City isn't just any country. It has a population of around only one thousand and covers less than half a square kilometer. This makes it the smallest country in the world. Vatican City is definitely small, but its history, art, and religious significance are huge. No wonder millions of people visit each year!
Amal looked up as Mr. Patel went to the front of the classroom.
"Listen up, class," he said. "I wanted to announce that we're going to put on a Thanksgiving play. We'll start rehearsing this week."
"A Thanksgiving play?" Keisha groaned. "That sounds babyish, Mr. Patel."
"It's not babyish," Mr. Patel said. "It's an excellent way to remind ourselves to be thankful for our blessings."
"Ooh! Ooh!" John waved his hand. "Can I play the turkey?"
"I want to be a cranberry!" Nathan said.

Everyone laughed so Amal joined in, even though she had no idea what was funny. Amal's family had moved from Syria last spring. She'd learned a lot about living in America, but many things were still confusing. Right now it was cranberries and turkeys that were baffling her.
A few other kids started complaining about the Thanksgiving play.
Mr. Patel held up his hand. "No more complaints. We're putting on a play, and you're all getting a part."
Amal bit her lip. That meant she was getting a part too.
The next day Mr. Patel had a stack of play scripts on his desk. He glanced at a list while he called out part assignments.
"Nathan and Keisha, you're going to play Native Americans."
"John, your wish is coming true—you get to be the turkey!"
"Amal, you're a Pilgrim, and—"
"A Pilgrim?" Amal repeated. "What's a Pilgrim?"
"Oh, Amal." Mr. Patel looked embarrassed. "I'm so sorry. Of course you're confused—this is your first American Thanksgiving."

"I'll explain how it started!" Nathan volunteered. He quickly explained that the Pilgrims were a group of people that left England in 1620. They sailed to America on the Mayflower , seeking religious freedom in the New World. After they resettled in America, they faced many difficulties such as harsh weather and illness. Lots of people died. But with the help of Native Americans, the Pilgrims learned how to adapt to their new land. The Native Americans taught the Pilgrims how to plant corn and where to fish and hunt.

"The following year was their first harvest," Nathan went on. "The surviving Pilgrims held a huge feast with the Native Americans. They gave thanks for their freedom and other blessings they'd found in America."
"So a Pilgrim was someone who traveled to a new place?" Amal asked.
"Yes, someone seeking a better life," Mr. Patel said.
"Why did your family leave Syria?" Keisha asked Amal.

"Because of the war." Amal swallowed hard. "Every night there were terrible bombings. Families started fleeing our city, and one day, my father said we had to leave too. We walked for hours, and planes were still dropping bombs. We were terrified that one would hit us!"
"Where did you go?" Nathan asked.
"We boarded a bus and traveled to a refugee camp in Jordan. We lived there for nine months until a mosque here offered to sponsor us. They said they could help us resettle in this town."
"Wow," John said. "Did your whole family resettle here?"
Amal shook her head. "My other relatives went to different refugee camps. We haven't seen anyone since we left."
Everyone was quiet.
"Resettling in America has been hard," Amal went on softly. "But many people are helping us. Someone found a job for my father, and volunteers are teaching English to my mother."
"Well, I think you're going to be a fantastic Pilgrim!" Nathan declared. "Just like the Thanksgiving Pilgrims, you left your home to start a brand-new life in a foreign country."
"That takes so much courage!" Keisha added.
Amal smiled as her classmates started applauding for her. "Life in America is often difficult," she thought. "But each day it gets a little easier."
Claudia hurried into the local TV station. As her prize for winning a local journalism contest, she was going to follow a TV news reporter for the entire day.
"This is going to be awesome!" she thought.
The first part of the day was a morning meeting. Claudia listened as the news director assigned news stories to reporters.
Afterward, a reporter named Meredith Burke approached Claudia. "You'll be working with me today."

Claudia forced a smile as she shook Meredith's hand. The reporter seemed very smart, but Claudia had been hoping to work with a reporter covering something exciting. Meredith had been assigned to a story with a boring topic—road repairs.

Meredith led Claudia over to her desk and reached for a phone. "First we have to schedule interviews with people who might be affected by the construction. You might be surprised to learn that a TV reporter spends a lot of time on the phone. Do you have any questions about the story?"
Claudia shook her head. She didn't feel interested enough in road construction to have any questions. Still, she tried to act polite and listen alertly as the reporter made the calls.
Finally Meredith hung up. "I've arranged to meet with some people in the area near the project. Let's find Jeremy, my videographer, and get in the van."
"Sounds good," Claudia mumbled.
At the roadwork site, Claudia saw construction workers and large vehicles everywhere.
"What do you think we should record, Claudia?" Meredith asked.
"Aren't you going to interview people?" Claudia asked.
"Yes, but we need to record more than just the interviews."
Jeremy nodded. "It would be pretty boring to show people talking about roadwork without showing the actual construction."
Claudia looked around as Jeremy began setting up his camera. "Well, maybe you could film around the whole construction site? And also get some close-ups of the road?"
Meredith smiled. "Smart ideas." She began giving more specific directions to Jeremy.
News stories on TV were usually only a couple of minutes long—but Jeremy recorded for much longer than that.
"We'll edit everything back at the TV station," Meredith explained. "Now it's time to interview some people. What questions should I ask?"
"Um . . . " Claudia thought. "Are you happy with the roadwork?"
"That's an okay way to start. But yes or no questions aren't very exciting for interviews. What about—"
"How do you feel about the roadwork?" Claudia burst out.
Meredith grinned and showed Claudia her notepad. "That's actually my first question!"
Throughout the morning Claudia observed as Meredith interviewed local residents and business owners. Everyone had an opinion on the construction.
"I'm glad the city is finally repairing the roads," one woman said. "It will improve my commute."
"We can't ride our bikes anymore," a kid complained. "And our bus stop got moved to a different street!"
"The construction is terrible for business," a restaurant owner said.

"I think this is enough," Meredith said after her sixth interview. "Now we need to record an introduction to the story. After seeing the site and doing some interviews, I think I know how to report the story to viewers."
Meredith and Jeremy planned out a few shots. Then she stood in front of the camera with a microphone. "Local residents have mixed reactions to roadwork on Renard Road . . . "
Back at the station, Meredith led Claudia to an editing room with computer monitors.

"We recorded about two hours of material. Now we're going to edit it down to a two-minute segment." Meredith showed Claudia how the software worked. After she'd finished the video segment, she recorded a few more lines of sound in a recording booth.
"Finished!"
"That was a ton of work for a two-minute story," Claudia said. "But it was really fun."
"Phew!" Meredith looked relieved. "I was afraid you might find a story about roadwork boring."
"Maybe at first," Claudia admitted. "But it certainly matters to the people in that neighborhood."
"Ready to see if the news desk has another story for us?" Meredith asked. "Reporters usually handle several stories in a day."
Claudia was already on her feet.
Callie hurried into the community center with her best friend, Allison, trailing after her.
"How did you ever convince me to join Teen Club?" Allison muttered.
"It'll be fun," Callie said. "And this summer is going to be so much better than last summer. Remember how we sat around every single day, doing nothing? It was so boring!"
"If you ask me," Allison said, "that's the whole point of summer break—doing nothing."

The girls joined some other teenagers sitting in a circle. The club leader, Sofia, asked everyone to introduce themselves, and then she told them about the club. "We're going to do lots of activities here in the city. But we'll also leave the city for some new adventures. Our first outing is next week, and I'd really like everyone to go. It will help us get to know each other."
Allison had perked up when Sofia mentioned adventures. "Where are we going?"
"Up to Treetop Mountain for a zip-line ride," Sofia said.
Allison gripped Callie's arm. "I've always wanted to zip-line," she whispered, "and I heard Treetop's course is awesome!"
Callie nodded and forced a smile, but "awesome" wasn't the word that had popped into her mind. Her word was "terrifying"!

Callie walked home slowly, preoccupied by the outing to Treetop. "I can't go zip-lining," she thought for the hundredth time. High places terrified her—she couldn't imagine flying high above trees on a rope! Nor could she imagine a way to get out of it—Sofia wanted the whole Teen Club to go. Plus, Allison was really excited, and Callie couldn't bear to let her down.

As Callie approached an apartment building, she put up a hand to shield her eyes from the sun. "Am I seeing a mirage," she joked, "or is that really Nate Garcia holding a book instead of a game controller?"

"Oh, it's me all right—the new and improved me." Nate rolled his eyes. "My grades dropped this year, so I've been ordered to do more reading. And I have to stop hanging out with my friends who play too many video games. What are you up to this summer?"
Callie told him about Teen Club.
Nate's mother abruptly stuck her head out of a window. "He'll join that club too. Nate needs to keep busy—and find the right friends!"

The following week Callie found herself staring out the window as the bus climbed the winding road up Treetop Mountain. The driver parked at the top, and the kids headed over to where Jeff, the guide, was waiting for them. Callie was trying to calm her nerves, but they weren't cooperating.

"Who's zip-lined before?" Jeff asked. Only Nate and another kid raised their hands. "No problem," Jeff continued, walking over to where the helmets and harnesses were. "I'm going to demonstrate exactly what to do."
After the lesson, everyone buckled on harnesses and helmets. Then they walked through the woods until they reached a platform where two zip-lines started.
"When it's your turn, I'll clip your harness to a cable," Jeff said. "When I say, 'now,' step forward, and keep your legs in front of you."

Soon Allison and Sofia were zooming off, whooping with delight. Callie stayed at the back of the line, pacing around as her heart pounded and her legs wobbled. She bent over, desperately trying to remember Jeff's instructions.
"Are you okay?"
Callie straightened up to see Nate gazing at her. "Not really," she confessed, "because I'm scared—really, really scared!"
"You can do it," Nate said.

Callie shook her head, but Nate kept reassuring her. "Just remind yourself that zip-lining is fun and safe, and take deep breaths. I'll be riding on the other zip-line, and afterward you'll be glad you tried it."
Jeff beckoned to Nate and Callie—it was their turn!

Nate took off first. Callie breathed deeply as Jeff clipped her harness to the cable. "Now!" he said, and Callie quickly stepped off the platform. "Whoa!" she cried as she bounded forward. "I'm flying!"

As cool air rushed past, she closed her eyes. When she opened them again, she gaped at the beautiful expanse spread out in front of her. Blue sky was everywhere, and below, the trees were a brilliant green canopy.
Allison and the others cheered as Callie reached the other side.
"I did it!" Callie cried, flashing Nate an exhilarated smile. As he grinned back, a new thought struck her: His eyes were as blue as the sky.

In 1874 around 3,500 curious people paid one franc to attend an Impressionist art exhibition in Paris. At this exhibition an unknown artist named Claude Monet showed his painting Impression, Sunrise to the public for the first time. Monet's painting was a scene of a harbor at sunrise, with noticeable brushstrokes swirling around the canvas in hazy colors. Other now-famous artists—Edgar Degas, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, and Berthe Morisot—also showed works at this exhibition. And how did the public react to their paintings? They laughed!

Since the 1600s the most important art exhibition in France had been the Salon. Every year artists submitted works to a jury of critics who selected the best paintings to exhibit. The Salon's decisions could make or break an artist's career. Acceptance meant publicity and opportunities for more work, but getting accepted was not easy.
The Salon had strict preferences. Paintings had to look realistic. Religious and historical themes were appreciated. Landscapes, still lifes, and contemporary scenes were not.

Before the Impressionists most painters focused on the Salon's preferred subjects, capturing them in paintings with dark colors. The painting techniques used by traditional artists hadn't changed much since the Renaissance over four hundred years earlier.

The world, however, was beginning to change in dramatic ways, which made the late nineteenth century an exciting time for artists. Painters could buy mass-produced paint in tubes, which was far more convenient than making their own. Japan began trading with Europe, which introduced new styles of art to the Western world. The city of Paris had been enlarged and modernized, and some artists were eager to modernize art as well.
However, one modern technology represented a growing challenge for artists: photography. Photographs had become widespread and could perfectly capture reality. Did anyone need paintings anymore?

The Impressionists believed they could compete with black-and-white photography by using their own unique tools—light and color. Most artists painted indoors in a studio. The Impressionists painted outdoors in the open air, or in the cafes and neighborhoods of the city. With quick, spontaneous brushstrokes, the Impressionists captured colorful impressions of everyday life as they saw them. Painting realistically didn't matter to the Impressionists, but it still mattered to the Salon, which rejected the Impressionists' work.

In 1863 the Salon rejected so many paintings that it became a public controversy. Public controversy could be dangerous in France. The angry public had removed kings, politicians, and an emperor before. Emperor Napoleon III did not want that to happen to him. He decided that the rejected works should be displayed to the public in a separate exhibition. It was called the Salon of the Refused, and it attracted a lot of attention. In fact, more people attended the Salon of the Refused than the Paris Salon! However, few people took the rejected paintings seriously.

The Impressionists were not discouraged by the poor reception. Instead they were delighted—the Salon of the Refused made the public aware of their work! The following year the Impressionists requested that another Salon of the Refused be held. But the French government refused their request. Further requests were also denied for the next decade. Impatient and determined, the Impressionists decided to hold their own exhibition in 1874.

Calling themselves the Anonymous Society of Artists, the Impressionists displayed 165 works. Monet, Renoir, Degas, and Morisot all participated. Time had not changed public opinion though. Upon seeing Impression, Sunrise , one critic wrote that it looked less finished than sketches for wallpaper.
Meanwhile the Impressionists did not give up on the Paris Salon. They continued to submit their work, and they continued to be rejected.

Between 1874 and 1886, the Impressionists held a total of eight independent exhibitions. By their third in 1877, they were officially calling themselves Impressionists. This show included Renoir's Ball at the Galette Windmill , a now-famous painting that sold for $78 million in 1990.

With each exhibition different artists displayed works, and something began to change: public opinion. People were gradually opening their eyes to the beauty of Impressionist art. Even the Salon began accepting the Impressionists' work, and artists like Monet finally achieved mainstream success.

Impressionism itself evolved as newer artists experimented with new techniques. Small, delicate brushstrokes were replaced with bold shapes by Paul Cezanne and Paul Gauguin. Georges-Pierre Seurat painted scenes made of tiny dots of paint. These painters eventually became known as Post-Impressionists. Later artists like Vincent van Gogh continued to experiment and develop their own unique styles.

Today the Impressionists are remembered as genius artists, respected as deeply as the realistic artists they rebelled against. Their paintings sell for millions of dollars. Just like in 1874, the Impressionists can draw large crowds to museums and galleries. But you won't hear anyone laughing at them anymore!
Sage peeled a banana—her favorite after-practice snack—as she and her best friend, Lourdes, walked out of Park Gymnastics.

"I can't believe the tryouts for Misty Blackwell's Gymnastics Camp are next Saturday," Sage said. For three years in a row, she had tried out for the camp run by former Olympian Misty Blackwell. But Misty, a six-time gold medalist, only chose gymnasts with Olympic potential. Since Sage's last rejection, she had been preparing for this year's tryouts. Her parents thought she put too much pressure on herself, but going to the Olympics had been Sage's dream forever.
"I'm so nervous about the tryouts," Lourdes said.
"You're going to make it this year," Sage said firmly. "You're the best gymnast at Park. Besides, it's our last chance—we'll be too old next year. Plus, maybe the camp will help us catch up to Emi!"

Emi Wilson was the top gymnast at Park's rival gym and had been to the camp three times already. "There's a rumor that Emi's going to train overseas this summer, so she's not trying out," Lourdes said.

Sage's face lit up. "Really?" She grinned. Emi's absence this year would definitely give Sage an advantage she had never had before. "I'll work extra hard this week to get one step closer to my dream!"
When Sage and Lourdes arrived at the tryouts, the gym was packed with gymnasts and spectators. The girls joined the line at the registration table just as Misty Blackwell walked past.
The famous gymnast stopped briefly to greet them. "I remember you two from last year—good luck with your tryouts."
Sage froze. "Thank you, Ms. Blackwell!"
"She remembered us!" Lourdes said.
"I need to make sure that she remembers my performance too," Sage said.
The girls took their seats and waited for the tryouts to start.
"First up," the announcer called, "Emi Wilson."
Lourdes gasped. "What's she doing here?"
"I guess the rumors were wrong," Sage mumbled.
As Sage watched Emi's performance, she could feel her anxiety mounting—Emi's technique was perfect. But Sage couldn't let it rattle her.
"If Emi can give a perfect performance, so can you," she told herself sternly. "You've worked hard all week for this!"
After Emi gave a final bow, the announcer called Sage to the floor.
Lourdes flashed her a sympathetic look. "It stinks that you have to go right after Emi."
Sage tried to brush it off. "I'm super prepared—Emi isn't the only one with Olympic potential."
"That's the right attitude!" Lourdes grinned. "Good luck!"

Sage walked onto the mat and breathed in deeply. As the music started, she raised her arms, striking a pose before tiptoeing backward to the edge of the mat. She was preparing for her first big move—a series of fast forward flips across the mat. But something instantly felt wrong . . . Had her last step been too wide? Yes—and her heel had gone out of bounds!
"Such a stupid mistake!" a voice in her head screamed. Quickly she tried to reassure herself. "You can make up for the error. Yesterday at practice your routine was perfect!"

With that, Sage began her running start for the first flip. Suddenly everything seemed to move in slow motion. Her right foot wasn't in position . . . her last step was awkward. She couldn't regain her balance. And then— bam! Sage flopped facedown onto the mat.
Gasps rose from the crowd, and tears sprang to Sage's eyes. She wanted to get up and run away, but years of competing had taught her that quitting was not an option.
As she picked herself up, the crowd applauded. She improvised a few poses, and then bravely continued her routine.
After the tryouts Sage sat in a booth at Frosty Spoon, staring at Lourdes' certificate.
Lourdes handed Sage a frozen yogurt, then discreetly slipped the certificate onto the seat, out of Sage's sight.
"Even the best gymnasts fall," Lourdes said.
Sage sighed. "I know. But even if I hadn't fallen, I wouldn't have gotten into Misty's camp."
"What?" Lourdes said. "But you were so prepared, and you've done so well in competitions this year."
"True," Sage agreed, "but there were lots of amazing gymnasts today—including you—all more talented than I am. My dream probably wasn't very realistic after all."
"But it's good to dream big!" Lourdes protested.
"Dreams are great," Sage said, "but not all dreams can come true."
"Does this mean you're going to quit gymnastics?"
"I'm not sure what it means yet," Sage said, "but I won't quit."
Lourdes looked sad and uncomfortable.
"I'm disappointed about my poor tryout," Sage added quickly, "but you know what—I'm going to be fine. Gymnastics might even be more fun without all the pressure I've been putting on myself."
"Good point," Lourdes said.
Sage dipped her spoon into the bowl of frozen yogurt. "Mmm," she said, smiling, "it's my favorite flavor—banana!"

Pete sat down at a table in the bookstore with a freshly baked chocolate-chip cookie. Abdul was already there, waiting for him to start their session. Pete was tutoring the younger boy, helping him with his English class. Pete was about to bite into the cookie when he noticed Abdul had only books in front of him today. "Abdul, aren't you getting a snack?"
Abdul shook his head. "It's Ramadan," he said quietly, "so I'm fasting."
Pete felt his face turn bright red. "Oh, sorry . . . " Quickly he changed the subject and put down the cookie. "What do you need to study for your exam?"
Abdul pointed to a handout filled with English words. He had written their Arabic definitions in the margin. "I'd like to review this vocabulary, as well as some possible essay questions."

While they reviewed material for Abdul's test, Pete was curious. He knew Ramadan was the holiest time of year for Muslims, the followers of Islam. Since Muslims made up nearly a quarter of the world's population, Ramadan was a big holiday in Islamic and even non-Islamic countries. But that was about all he knew.
When they took a break, Pete asked Abdul to tell him more about Ramadan.

"Ramadan commemorates the time when a prophet named Muhammad received important teachings from Allah—that's the name for God in our religion," Abdul explained. "Muhammad recorded those teachings in the Qur'an, the holy book of Islam."
As Pete listened to Abdul, his stomach rumbled with hunger—he still hadn't eaten his snack. "How long is Ramadan?"
"It's one lunar month. We observe Ramadan during the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, and it begins when the new moon arrives."
"How do you survive while fasting for a whole month?" Pete asked.

Abdul laughed. "We eat a little, but only before sunrise and after sunset. In fact, the whole month is named Ramadan, which means . . . " He thought for a second. "'Burning heat.' The burning can mean the burning of fasting. Or it can mean the burning away of sins by fasting."
"Do all Muslims fast for Ramadan?" Pete asked.

"Sick people and young children don't," Abdul explained. "I started fasting gradually, for brief periods, when I was around ten years old. But Ramadan isn't just about fasting. We also pray more and perform charitable deeds such as helping others or donating food and money. Good deeds are important to our faith."
"It must be hard to fast for a month," Pete said.

Abdul eyed Pete's tray. "Please, Pete, eat your snack. Fasting is hard, but I'm used to it. Besides, this is a sacred time for me. During Ramadan I grow closer to my family and Allah. I also gain more compassion for those who are suffering. I believe this makes me a stronger person and a better Muslim."
Pete nodded and took a few bites of the cookie before quietly wrapping it in a napkin and slipping it into his backpack.
"You seem very curious about Ramadan," Abdul said. "Would you like to join my family for our iftar tomorrow night? That's the meal we eat after sunset."
"I'd love to come," Pete said.
"Great," Abdul said with a smile. "In the meantime we'd better get back to studying. I want to do well on my exam."
After dark the next evening, Pete knocked on Abdul's door.
"Welcome, Pete!" Abdul said. He gestured toward a mat where the family kept their shoes.
Pete slipped off his shoes and then turned to greet Abdul's parents. "Thank you for inviting me."
Abdul's father shook Pete's hand. "Thank you for coming, Pete."
"It is our pleasure to share our iftar with you," Abdul's mother said, smiling warmly.

Soon Abdul's mother was bringing out platters of food. Pete followed the family's lead by eating very slowly at first, taking just a date and a few sips of water. Then he helped himself to some delicious-looking meat kebabs, vegetable salad, and yogurt.
"We will get up before dawn and eat another meal," Abdul said. "That one is called sahoor ."
"When does Ramadan end?" Pete asked.

"Ramadan ends when the next new moon arrives," Abdul replied. "And when Ramadan is over, we break our fast with a three-day holiday—Eid al-Fitr. During Eid al-Fitr, we eat many delicious foods and gather together to pray."
Just then Abdul's grandfather entered the room. His eyes lit up when Abdul introduced Pete as his tutor.
"So you are the famous Pete! You are doing a great job as Abdul's tutor. Thank you for teaching him so well."
"Abdul is a very good student," Pete said, "but he's also an excellent teacher. Thanks to him, I've learned all about Ramadan!"
"Finally, PE!" Briana began doing warm-up stretches.
"I wonder what we'll do today," Ally said. It had been too snowy for the past month to hold PE outside.
"I don't care. Anything is better than history class," Briana said. "It's so boring!"
Mrs. Farrow, the PE teacher, entered the gymnasium carrying two large trash cans and a soccer ball.
"Are we playing soccer inside?" Miguel asked hopefully.
"That doesn't explain the trash cans," Briana said.
Mrs. Farrow grinned. "We are having a history lesson!"
"No! Not history!" Briana moaned.

Mrs. Farrow ignored the complaint. "It was a snowy winter in Massachusetts in 1891," she began. "Too snowy for baseball or football. A group of college students was stuck inside for every PE class, so their teacher invented a new game for them to play. Today we're going to play that game!"
"This might be better than regular history class," Briana thought.

"The teacher's name was James Naismith," Mrs. Farrow said. "He based his idea on a throwing game from his childhood in Canada. The targets he decided on were peach baskets, but these are the best I can do." She gestured to the trash cans. "Now, to get them in place."

The custodian brought a ladder and fastened a trash can high on the gym wall. The kids laughed at the sight. As the custodian put another trash can on the opposite wall, Mrs. Farrow divided the students into teams of nine.

"The point of the game is to get the ball into your opposing team's trash can," Mrs. Farrow explained. "You cannot run with the ball or touch the other players. Whichever team scores the most goals wins."
"That sounds like basketball," Briana said.
"Exactly!" Mrs. Farrow said.
"But why do you have a soccer ball?" Ally asked.

"Early basketball players used soccer balls," the teacher answered. "Real basketballs weren't made until 1894. They were made from leather and stitched together." She patted the soccer ball. "Ready for the tip-off?"

Briana faced off against Miguel. Basketball was her favorite game, but she never thought it had any connection to history! The teacher tossed the ball high, and both kids leaped for it. Briana made contact first, sending the ball straight to Ally. Ally dribbled— tweet! The whistle sounded.
"I forgot to mention dribbling the ball wasn't allowed until 1909," Mrs. Farrow said. "The only way to move the ball is to pass it to someone else."
They started again. Briana caught a pass from Kevin, the soccer ball feeling strangely soft and light in her hands. She shot the ball over Miguel's head. It clanged into the trash can.
Ally gave her a high five. "You're better at history than you thought!"
"First goal!" Mrs. Farrow said. "Now we just need to get the ball back . . . "
The players waited while the teacher climbed the ladder and retrieved the ball.
"Don't make too many goals!" the teacher joked.
"Real baskets are definitely better than trash cans—or peach baskets!" Briana said.
After another fifteen minutes, Miguel's team was in the lead by one goal. Mrs. Farrow blew her whistle again to signal the end of play.
"Whew!" Briana was breathing hard but grinning. "That was a good game."
Mrs. Farrow gathered the class together. "What do you think of old-school basketball?"
"It's hard not to dribble the ball," Miguel said.
"And it's strange to have more than five on a team," Ally added.
"A lot is the same though," Briana said. "Making baskets, passing the ball, not touching the other players . . . "
The teacher nodded. "Mr. Naismith wanted to make a game that was all about skill and strategy, not force."
Briana smiled. "I still prefer modern basketball. But the old-school game was fun."
"Does that mean you like history now?" Mrs. Farrow asked.
Briana laughed. "Not exactly!"

The sun sets. Wolves howl at the rising moon. Owls' hoots echo through the night. Bats swoop through the darkness on silent wings. These creatures of the night are the stuff of spooky legends—and scary movies. But is there any truth to the legends surrounding these animals?

Long ago it was frightening to hear wolves howling at night. Wolves were seen as dangerous beasts, and people who did horrible things were thought of as beasts. So legends arose of werewolves—people who turned into wolf-like beasts during a full moon. These werewolves had sharp fangs and claws and hairy bodies. They remained vicious beasts until the sun rose, when they returned to their human forms and personalities.

Today we know that werewolves aren't real. We also know that wolves don't howl at night to be scary. Wolves are nocturnal, so they're awake at night. They howl to communicate with their pack or stake out territory. Pointing their noses toward the sky helps their sounds carry for a long distance—9 to 16 kilometers. Despite the legends, wolves don't howl more during full moons. People were just more likely to see wolves under the light of a full moon!

The hoot of the owl also struck terror in people long ago. As with wolves, spooky legends arose about these mysterious nighttime creatures. In some legends witches turned into owls at night. Many cultures saw owls as a symbol of death. In Europe, for example, people believed that an owl nearby meant someone would die. When they heard the owl hoot, they hoped its big shiny eyes were not watching them!

Luckily owls don't hoot at night as messengers of doom. Owls, like wolves, are nocturnal. They hoot to communicate with other owls. They may hoot to claim territory or talk to a mate or their chicks. Sometimes their hoots are warnings. But these aren't warnings of death. These warning hoots let other owls know there are people nearby! Why do owls have such large eyes that glow in the darkness? Since owls hunt at night, their eyes help them see. Owls can also turn their necks so they can see backwards. This helps them silently track their prey.

Another creature of legend is the vampire bat—the strange flying mammal that sucks blood. Surprisingly, legends about vampires didn't come from vampire bats. People from Ancient Egypt, Tibet, and Rome had stories about vampires who sucked blood. Much later, European explorers discovered bats in Mexico and Central America that lived off blood. They named these bats vampire bats after the legendary creatures. The legend about human vampires turning into vampire bats began even later. That legend is from Dracula , the famous horror novel. The character Dracula could turn into a bat and fly through the night.

But unlike vampires from legends, vampire bats don't really suck blood. Vampire bats usually approach their targets from the ground. They use their sharp teeth to pierce the skin of their prey. Then they drink the flowing blood using their tongues. They don't kill their victims—or turn them into vampires! And vampire bats rarely prey on humans. They usually feed on cattle and horses.

People have always tried to explain the unknown. Legends help to explain mysterious things that people encounter. Now we know that some legends aren't true, but people still enjoy a good scary story. When the moon rises, filling the night with shadows, it's fun to pretend legends are real!
Hi Marcus,

I hope you like your new school, but I really miss you here! This year the drama club is putting on William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet . You probably think I'm playing Romeo since I'm usually the lead in drama club productions.
But you're wrong.

I'm not even in the cast! Mrs. Geller picked me for stage manager. I'll be in charge of the sets, sound and lighting, and props. She said it would be good experience, but it sounds pretty boring to me. And you know what makes it even worse? Rose Adams is playing Juliet! This would have been my chance to get to know her better. Instead I'm stuck backstage, and Jae gets to be Romeo.
I guess it's good that you moved all the way across the country. Things around here aren't much fun.
Hope to hear from you soon!
Carlos
Hey!

Sorry it's been so long since I wrote. I've been super busy! The sets for the play are supposed to be pretty basic. But we've been working every single afternoon to build what we need. We just finished the set for the scene where Juliet talks to Romeo from her balcony. I came up with the idea for the set. We painted big pieces of cardboard to look like the front of Juliet's house. Then we cut out a doorway and added a railing. Rose stands on a platform behind the cardboard front. It looks just like she's looking over a balcony railing!

We're making props too. We used wood for daggers and painted the blades with shiny silver paint. Jae's little brother lent us a giant plastic baseball bat. We covered it with brown paper to make it look like a wooden club for the fight scene in act 1. It's actually fun thinking of ways to make things or adapt them to look realistic for the props.
I have to run now. We're meeting in a few minutes to discuss sound and lighting.
Talk to you soon!
Carlos

I don't know how we're going to get everything done in two weeks! The cast is rehearsing every afternoon, and the backstage crew is working long hours too. If we don't get the sets, lighting, and sound just right, the play will be ruined.

I've learned how to set up the sound system so even people in the rear of the theater can hear everything. If there wasn't a sound system, the actors would need to yell! Lighting is tricky too. Without it, the audience wouldn't be able to see much onstage. You have to aim the light where the action is. It's taken some practice to make sure we move the lights up and down on cue.

And you're not going to believe this: Jae broke his leg playing soccer, so he's out of the play! Mrs. Geller asked me to replace him since I've been helping him with his lines and know almost all of them. But I've just gotten the hang of working the sound system. Working backstage is more fun than I thought, and there's still a lot to do. We have to design and print programs, put up posters to advertise the play, and take care of so many more details. Luckily Mrs. Geller said Larry could play Romeo if I help him practice. Whew! Thank you, Larry!
Carlos
Hey Marcus!

Too bad you couldn't come! The play sold out and the audience loved it. I think this is our best drama club production ever. We still have six more performances and they're all sold out. I hope I get to work backstage again next year.
Well, I have to rush off to the after-play party. I was talking to Juliet/Rose between scenes, and she said she hoped to see me there. Just call me backstage Romeo!

14.title: Pale Male: A Hawk Survives in New York City

paragraphs.text: Look, up in the sky! Is it a bird? Is it a plane? It's a red-tailed hawk! They call him Pale Male because he has a large patch of white feathers on his chest, and he is male. He came out of nowhere to try to make it in the big city. He is brave and fearless.

There are many birds that live in New York City's Central Park. In 1990, 215 different species lived there—but no hawks. Then, in the fall of 1991, Pale Male appeared. He was the first hawk to make his home in Central Park, the most visited city park in the United States. Hawks usually live in the open countryside, so people were very excited to see him. They enjoyed watching him hunt for rats, pigeons, and squirrels from high atop his perch.

Red-tailed hawks like to watch for prey—the creatures that other animals kill and eat—from the tops of tall trees. But since Pale Male lived in the city, his favorite perches were the tops of apartment buildings! Fifth Avenue, which lines Central Park, is where many rich and famous people live. Pale Male sat on their balconies. When he saw a rat or pigeon on the ground, he would swoop down to catch it. People were amazed that a hawk could survive this way in the city.

People were even more amazed when, the next spring, Pale Male brought a mate to New York. Together they built a nest in a tall tree in the park. But crows, a natural enemy of red-tailed hawks, drove the pair away. What would they do?

Pale Male had an idea. He and his mate broke twigs from a tree and flew to the top of a 12-story apartment building. They built their nest on a ledge above someone's apartment window! They chose a good spot. The spikes on the ledge helped keep the nest firmly in place. And the ledge gave them a great view of the park.

Soon the family grew. When three chicks were seen in the nest, people watching below cheered. They had been waiting a long time to see the chicks. Pale Male and his mate fed the baby chicks every day. When the babies were ready, they learned to fly from their parents. Pale Male and his mate were good parents.

Pale Male was becoming more and more famous. A devoted group of bird-watchers followed his every move. New Yorkers grew to love him as they read about his adventures in the newspapers and saw pictures of him and his family on the Internet. He became a part of everyday life in the city.

But not everyone loved the hawks. Red-tailed hawks are large birds, and they keep adding twigs to their nests. The apartment people didn't like the mess they made. Pale Male's nest was now eight feet wide and weighed four hundred pounds! People complained that bits of the nest and pigeon parts kept falling to the ground. They wanted to get rid of the nest.
One cold and rainy day in December 2004, the apartment people got permission to take down the nest. Pale Male's home was gone.

The next day everyone knew what had happened. It was in the newspapers and on TV all over the world. Soon people gathered at the building to protest. They carried signs: HONK 4 HAWKS! NYC KIDS FOR PALE MALE! BRING BACK THE NEST! Cars, buses, cabdrivers, even police in their cruisers honked in support as they drove by.

People who loved Pale Male wrote letters to the apartment people. It took about three weeks, but finally the two groups met. The hawk lovers won. Pale Male could now build a new nest. Experts were called in to design a better support structure for it, one that would make everyone happy.

And the happiest of all was—Pale Male, of course! As of 2014 he is still living on the ledge in New York City. He has raised many chicks with all of his mates. There are even books and movies about Pale Male.
Now that's a pretty amazing story!

The Great Wall of China is one of the most recognizable landmarks in the world. It is the world's longest structure. In fact, some astronauts have said they could see it from space! Curving across the land like a sleeping dragon, it follows almost the entire northern border of China for more than twenty thousand kilometers.

You might ask why a nation would need a wall along its border. The Chinese people built the Great Wall to protect their civilization from attacking tribes in the north. But the Great Wall of China took over two thousand years to complete, and during this time an incredible amount of history unfolded.
Qin Dynasty (221 BC to 206 BC)

The Qin dynasty was a short-lived but important dynasty because its first ruler, Emperor Qin Shi Huang, was a very influential emperor. He unified China and started the construction of the Great Wall of China. He used all his authority to get the wall built.

The builders used the hang-tu method of construction. They erected two temporary barriers parallel to each other and packed a layer of dirt, stones, and wood between them. After many layers were built up, the temporary barriers were removed, leaving a tall, thick earthen wall. Watchtowers were constructed along the wall so that soldiers could see enemy armies approaching. If invaders attacked, the soldiers lit a fire, and the smoke was a signal to warn the soldiers in the other watchtowers.

Back then there were no mechanical tools to help with construction, so all the work was done by hand. It was back-breaking labor, and life was very hard for the workers, especially because Emperor Qin was ruthless. It is believed that hundreds of thousands of men died building it.
The Qin dynasty did not last very long after the death of Emperor Qin Shi Huang in 210 BC. According to some accounts, he was able to build over 2,500 kilometers of the Great Wall.
Han Dynasty (206 BC to 220 AD)

After the fall of the Qin dynasty, a leader named Liu Bang came to power and established the Han dynasty. By the time Emperor Wu Di, the seventh emperor of the Han dynasty, came to power in 141 BC, the Great Wall had deteriorated and needed major repairs. Wu Di wanted to rebuild and extend the wall. His workers also used the hang-tu method of construction, so the architecture of the wall changed very little from that of the section built during the Qin dynasty. Wu Di's workers, however, had better working conditions, and got paid for their service. During Wu Di's reign, another large section of the Great Wall was completed.

It was also during the reign of Wu Di that China started trading its riches with countries in the west. Chinese traders traveled to Central Asia, the Middle East, and even as far as Rome, bringing silk, paper, and spices to Europe. This long trading route was called the Silk Road, and the main route of the Silk Road closely followed the curves of the Great Wall.

Life in villages along the wall was prosperous and peaceful during this time, but this era eventually came to an end. After the death of Emperor Wu Di in 87 BC, the Han dynasty slowly deteriorated and finally ended in 220 AD. It wasn't until a thousand years later, during the Ming dynasty, that the Great Wall became an impressive structure once again.
The Ming Dynasty (1368 AD to 1644 AD)

What we see of the Great Wall today was built during the Ming dynasty. The first emperor and his successors maintained the Great Wall very carefully, and strengthened it to keep invaders out. The wall became an important project for each of the Ming emperors.

By the time of this dynasty, new inventions had become available to help the workers with construction. Workers still used the hang-tu method of construction, but this time they packed the dirt and stones between two solid brick walls to make it more stable. They made the top of the wall wide enough for horse carriages to travel, and built more watchtowers. Now, instead of smoke signals, soldiers used gunpowder rockets to warn of an approaching enemy.

Another improvement made to the wall during the Ming dynasty was a drainage system. Until then rainwater slowly collected in the wall, making it deteriorate more quickly. After the last Ming emperor died in 1620, construction on the wall ceased. The era had ended.
From the Qing Dynasty to Today

For the next four centuries, China was ruled by the Qing dynasty, which did not need the wall to protect its borders. By the time the Qing dynasty collapsed and the Communist Party took control, the Great Wall was nearly forgotten. But in 1980 the Chinese government decided to restore the Great Wall and show it to the world. Today it is one of the most visited tourist attractions on earth, a silent witness to the many battles, wars, and changing empires of China's history.

16.title: The Suez Canal: The Impossible Dream

paragraphs.text: The story of the Suez Canal is a story of determination. It started as a simple idea, turned into a grand dream, and finally became a reality. The man behind this dream was a French diplomat named Ferdinand de Lesseps.

Born in France in 1805, Ferdinand was a bright, young man with a promising future. His father was a diplomat who worked in many countries around the world. Ferdinand studied to become a diplomat like his father, and in 1832 he was sent to Egypt to take a diplomatic job as the French consul at Alexandria.

Upon his arrival in the ancient city, however, Ferdinand had to stay in a hospital because someone from his ship had fallen sick. While he and others from the ship waited to learn if they were sick too, Ferdinand grew restless and picked up a book to read. The book was a report written by a French engineer, and reading it inspired a dream that Ferdinand pursued for the rest of his life.

The report was about building a waterway between the Mediterranean and Red seas. At that time ships sailing between Europe and Asia had to travel around the entire continent of Africa. If built, this new route would greatly shorten the trip between Europe and the Far East.

The report stated that building a canal from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea was impossible because of the different water levels of the two seas. But this conclusion did not discourage Ferdinand. Instead, as soon as the young consul was released from the hospital, he began researching the narrow piece of land, called the Isthmus of Suez, that separated the two seas.

Ferdinand discovered that the pharaohs of Ancient Egypt had built waterways to connect the Nile River to the Red Sea to have access to the rich copper mines and spice lands of East Africa. Unfortunately, this was thousands of years in the past, and those waterways were long lost. But now that he knew a similar canal had once been built, Ferdinand was more determined than ever to pursue his goal.

Ferdinand de Lesseps’ duties as the French consul were demanding. He traveled frequently between Alexandria and Cairo, and had little time for his beloved Suez Canal project. It was also difficult to get the ruler of Egypt to support his plans, even though Ferdinand was teaching French and horseback riding to the ruler’s grandson. Still Ferdinand did not give up. He continued to study the height of the land and the water levels along possible routes for the canal.

In 1837 Ferdinand was transferred from Egypt back to Europe to take up other diplomatic posts. He was sad to leave, and it was twenty years before he saw his beloved Egypt again. During those years, as his diplomatic responsibilities increased, his dream of the canal began to fade. In 1849 Ferdinand retired and went to live in a villa on the outskirts of Paris. It seemed to him that his great dream belonged to a part of his life that was over, but things were about to change.
One morning in 1854, Ferdinand was reading the newspaper when a headline caught his eye.

He read that Abbas Pasha, the ruler of Egypt, was dead and that Said Pasha had inherited the position. Said Pasha was the boy Ferdinand had taught back in Alexandria. The young prince was now a grown man who remembered the retired French consul fondly. Ferdinand knew that the new ruler of Egypt would support him in building the canal. His dream was coming to life once again. When Said invited Ferdinand to come to Egypt to celebrate his new position, Ferdinand promptly agreed.

In the time since Ferdinand’s first posting to Egypt, the reports about the different water levels of the Mediterranean and Red seas had been proved wrong. Now the only obstacle was finding the money to build the canal. Almost everyone thought Ferdinand was out of his mind to dig a canal in the desert, and he had a hard time finding financial supporters. But his diplomatic charm, optimism, and belief in the project prevailed. Ferdinand traveled between Europe and Egypt, gathering support for his project. It took him five years, but he was able to find supporters in France and Egypt who bought shares in his newly-formed Suez Canal Company. In 1859 he finally had enough funds to start digging; construction began in April of that year.

Once construction started, it took ten years of hard labor to complete the canal. Said Pasha supplied Ferdinand with the many laborers he needed. A total of one and a half million laborers worked on the canal, mostly by hand, digging in the sandy soil in extremely hot weather with almost no machinery to aid them. Finally, after much hardship and the death of many laborers, the Suez Canal was completed in 1869.

The day the Suez Canal officially opened, there was a grand celebration. Important people from all over the world came to Egypt, including Empress Eugenie of France. It had taken Ferdinand over forty years of hard work, but his dream had been realized. Europe and the Far East were finally connected.

The Suez Canal, one of the longest in the world, is 166 kilometers long, 11 meters deep, and 60 meters wide. It can accommodate any ship except the largest supertankers. Each year thousands of ships from almost every country in the world travel through the canal. In fact, 14 percent of all the goods traded worldwide pass through this waterway. Ferdinand’s dream to connect the world took him on a long and difficult journey, but in the end, the determined French diplomat succeeded.

17.title: Festivals of India: A Celebration of Life!

paragraphs.text: India is one of the oldest countries in the world. This fascinating place has a diverse and colorful history. Almost one-fifth of the entire world’s population lives in India; it is the second most populous country on earth, after China! Its geography is as diverse as its people. It has high mountains in the north, dry deserts in the west, and tropical beaches in the south. The people of India have adapted to life in all these different climates, and this is reflected in their culture, heritage, and language.

The people of India love to celebrate life. They are proud of their rich traditions and vibrant culture, and love to gather to celebrate any occasion. This is why they have many different festivals. There are hundreds of festivals all across India every month. There are so many that there is a holiday for every day of the year. Some festivals last only a day, some one week, and some last a whole month! Most often, Indian people celebrate the changing of the seasons, the beginning of the harvest, the full moon, and the arrival of rain. They also honor religious and national holidays such as the birthdays of saints, national heroes, and gurus. Each festival has a different name and is celebrated in a different way.
Holi, the Festival of Colors

One of the most popular festivals in India is the festival of Holi. This festival marks the end of winter and the beginning of the first harvest. It is usually celebrated at the end of February or the beginning of March. It starts on the night of the first full moon of spring. People begin to celebrate by lighting large bonfires in the middle of their towns to scare away evil spirits and ghosts. The following morning they run around the streets spraying each other with brightly colored powders and colored water. This is a time when people forget their worries and have fun. Everyone gets completely covered in a rainbow of colors. Around lunchtime the celebrations end, and people head to the river to wash off. They spend the rest of the day at home with their families.
Diwali, the Festival of Lights

Another popular festival is Diwali, or the festival of lights. All people─rich and poor, old and young, men and women─celebrate it. It is a four-day-long celebration, during which people decorate their homes with lanterns and set beautiful candles adrift on rivers or the ocean. By lighting lanterns, people thank their gods for giving them health, happiness, children, and knowledge. Diwali gives people a chance to scare away dark spirits and welcome light into their lives. The festival ends with a beautiful fireworks display at night.
Makar Sankranti, the Festival of Kites

A festival called Makar Sankranti celebrates the end of the long winter when the sun enters the northern hemisphere, which occurs on January 14. The sky fills up with hundreds of colorful shapes as people gather to fly kites, each one more beautiful than the next. People receive prizes for the most original kite or for flying their kite with the most skill. At night, people light lanterns, attach them to their kites, and fill the night sky with thousands of glowing lights.
Gandhi Festival

Each year on October 2, the people of India gather to celebrate the birth of their national hero, Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi fought to free India from British rule without violence. He led peaceful marches throughout the country and united the people of India. On this national holiday, people visit the many statues of Gandhi all around India and sing Gandhi’s favorite songs.
Yugadi, the Hindu New Year

Yugadi is the New Year celebration in the Hindu calendar. Each year it falls on a different day between March and April. It is a day of forgiveness and new beginnings. On the day of the holiday, people exchange sweets and ask each other for forgiveness. It is a day when merchants and accountants pay their debts as well.
Dasara, the Festival of Good and Evil

Dasara is a ten-day festival that celebrates the victory of good over evil. It is held in the town of Mysore in October. The whole town celebrates with concerts and dances. People decorate their homes with lanterns, candles, and flowers for nine days. On the tenth day, everyone dresses up in a colorful costumes and dances all around the town. This carnival is a rich celebration full of musicians, clowns, decorated elephants, and traditional dancers.

The people of India are proud of their country’s heritage, and this pride shows in the way they celebrate life. By honoring their traditions with colorful festivals, they show their respect and appreciation for India’s rich and varied culture. Every day is a festival of a different kind, making India a very exciting place!

The Leaning Tower of Pisa is one of the architectural wonders of the world, and permanently fascinating to people. The famous bell tower has stood for over six centuries. But it hasn't ever stood straight—at one point in history, the tower tilted about 4.5 meters from the vertical!
Pisa is an ancient city in Tuscany, Italy. Located on the river Arno, with easy access to the sea, the city became a major port of trade.
In the eleventh century, merchants from across the Mediterranean and as far away as the Middle East came to buy and sell goods.

The city's inhabitants, the Pisans, often had to defend their city against outside forces. They also made their own conquests. In 1063 they sailed to the island of Sicily and attacked the city of Palermo. The defeat of Palermo made the Pisans rich and confident in their power. They decided to build a large cathedral to show off their treasures.

A large piece of open land sat in the middle of the city, which the Pisans called the Square of Miracles. They decided to build the cathedral on the square, as a tribute to Pisa’s conquests and rich heritage. The front of the building was covered with stones stolen from ancient Roman ruins. Even today you can read ancient Roman inscriptions, some of which are upside down or sideways, in the marble stones of the cathedral. The building took a very long time to complete, almost three hundred years.

The Pisans also decided to build a cemetery and a tall bell tower in the square. Construction of the bell tower, which would later become known as the Leaning Tower of Pisa, began in 1173. Not long after the workers had laid the foundation and built the first three floors, they noticed that the building was sinking on the south side. This was not surprising because the soil underneath the Square of Miracles was very marshy. It was a common problem for buildings in the area. In fact, the name Pisa means "marshy land" in Greek.

Around this time war broke out, and construction on the bell tower stopped for nearly one hundred years. This long interruption turned out to be good for the tilting tower. It gave the building's foundation time to settle, and probably even prevented it from collapsing long ago.

Experts believe that when construction on the tower restarted, an engineer named Bonanno Pisano was in charge of the challenging project. In order to compensate for the building's tilt, Pisano decided to make the columns and arches on the south side a little longer. He believed that this would level out the tower. But Pisano's solution only worsened the problem. The extra weight made the tower sink some more!

As years passed, other engineers and builders took on the challenge of finishing the building, and fixing its tilt. By 1350 the tower’s bell chamber had been constructed, and the rest of the tower was finally completed around 1372.

When the tower was finished, many people were glad that all the builders had not quit the project. It was truly an architectural wonder, with beautiful arches and two hundred marble columns. But by now the tower's tilt was very noticeable. The tilt fascinated people, yet it worried them too; one day the tower could collapse.

Over time many efforts were made to save the tower. Some of the solutions were realistic, while others were almost comical. One person suggested draining all of the water beneath the foundation of the tower; another suggested leaving the water there but freezing it! Other ideas included moving the tower to another location or rebuilding it. In the 1920s experts tried injecting cement into the foundation of the tower in order to stabilize it, or at least slow the rate at which it was tilting.

Despite all these engineering efforts, the tower continued sinking. By the 1960s the Italian government was so concerned about the tower, they announced that they were looking for suggestions to solve this puzzling problem.

Finally, in 1990, it was decided to close the building for safety reasons. A major project was eventually launched to straighten the tower. This time engineers slowly removed earth from underneath the foundation on its north side. When the tower reopened in 2001, the tilt had been reduced by about 44 centimeters! And over time the tilt decreased even more.

The tall tower, with its unusual tilt, has fascinated not just builders and tourists. Galileo Galilei, a former resident of Pisa, was born about two hundred years after the tower was finished. He used it to conduct many important scientific experiments. In one famous story, Galileo wanted to prove his theory that all objects fall at the same speed. So he climbed to the top of the Tower of Pisa and dropped two balls at the same time. According to the story, both balls hit the ground at the same time even though they differed in weight.

Today the bell tower continues to draw tourists and admirers from around the world. Engineers believe, due to recent measurements, that the building will remain stable now for at least two hundred years. So for generations to come, people can continue to look in amazement at the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

I'm here in Egypt, standing on the Giza Plateau, which is known for its massive pyramids. The pyramid closest to me is the Pyramid of Khafre, named for the pharaoh who built it. The farther one is called the Great Pyramid of Giza. The Pharaoh Khufu—Khafre's father—built that one. You might find this hard to believe, but these pyramids were built over four thousand years ago.
Hidden in the gray dawn, there's something else. Do you see it? It's the back of a massive head! You're looking at the Great Sphinx of Giza!

You've probably already heard of the Great Sphinx of Giza. It's the tallest stone statue ever built in ancient Egypt. Scientists believe it was created around 2500 BC, maybe during Pharaoh Khafre's reign. Carved from limestone, the statue has a lion’s body and a person's head. The Great Sphinx really is "great"; its massive body is about 73 meters long and 20 meters high. Its head is bigger than a mansion, and its body weighs about the same as fifty jumbo jets!

The sphinx, a mythological creature, first appeared in ancient Egyptian and Greek culture. In art and stories, the sphinx always has a lion's body and a human's face. But while the ancient Greeks portrayed the sphinx as female, usually with wings, the ancient Egyptians portrayed the sphinx as male. Many Egyptian temples and pyramids have sphinx statues standing guard; the ancient Egyptians probably saw them as benevolent protectors.

The appearance of the sphinx in culture has given scientists clues about the Great Sphinx monument. But many mysteries still surround it. For instance, scholars wonder about the Sphinx's face. Was it carved to look like a real person? Perhaps Pharaoh Khafre or his father, Pharaoh Khufu? Many experts suspect the Sphinx has Khafre's face. That's because Khafre had a beard, and so did the statue, originally.

Why was the statue built? Maybe it was constructed to honor the pharaoh—a symbol of his awesome power. Or perhaps it was put there, facing east, to worship the sun.
